claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chucair-Elliott et al., 2017b and Conrady et al., 2013.

claims.claim: CD4 T cells coordinate corneal sensation loss in HSV-1 keratitis.
claims.source: Moreover, CD4 T cells coordinate this pathology. Our data corroborate findings from the Hendricks' lab showing that CD4 T cells are associated with corneal sensation loss in HSV-1 keratitis (Yun et al., 2014), yet our adoptive transfer experiments establish that this process is not dependent upon endogenous C3 production by cornea-infiltrating donor T cells (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to Yun et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Corneal sensation loss in HSV-1 keratitis is not dependent upon endogenous C3 production by cornea-infiltrating T cells.
claims.source: Our data corroborate findings from the Hendricks' lab showing that CD4 T cells are associated with corneal sensation loss in HSV-1 keratitis (Yun et al., 2014), yet our adoptive transfer experiments establish that this process is not dependent upon endogenous C3 production by cornea-infiltrating donor T cells (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer experiments showing C3-/- T cells can induce sensation loss in C3-sufficient recipients.

claims.claim: The tempo of HSV-associated sensation loss was consistent among models once initiated.
claims.source: Notably, the tempo of HSV-associated sensation loss was consistent among models once initiated (Figure 1B, Figure 2D, Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of sensation loss kinetics across different experimental models.

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of T cell numbers in different experimental groups.

claims.claim: Corneal sensation loss in HSV-1 infection and ocular GVHD share a common mechanism dependent upon CD4+ T cells and complement C3.
claims.source: Corneal sensation loss in HSV-1 infection and ocular GVHD shared a common mechanism dependent upon CD4+ T cells and complement C3.
claims.evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from both disease models.

claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Mice do not express CD46.
claims.source: However, mice do not express CD46.
claims.evidence: This reflects established knowledge about species differences in complement regulation.

claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Strainic et al., 2008.

claims.evidence: This is supported by the in vitro stimulation data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.source: Others have shown similar data based on T cell proliferation in response to re-stimulation with HSV-1 antigen (Da Costa et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Da Costa et al., 1999.

claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liszewski et al., 2013.

claims.evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms.

claims.source: The precise relationships between T cells and C3 in our mouse models of corneal neuropathic disease remain to be identified.
claims.evidence: This identifies a limitation and future direction.

claims.claim: The working hypothesis involves an indirect mechanism whereby sublytic MAC deposition from local complement activation damages sensory nerves, which are then cleared by T cell-activated phagocytes or other cytolytic cells.
claims.source: Our working hypothesis involves an indirect mechanism whereby sublytic MAC deposition from local complement activation damages sensory nerves, which are then cleared by T cell-activated phagocytes or other cytolytic cells.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic model based on the findings.

claims.claim: Tissue-resident and infiltrating leukocytes as well as nerve-associated corneal epithelial cells could be involved in clearing damaged nerves.
claims.source: These could include tissue-resident and infiltrating leukocytes (macrophages, monocytes, dendritic cells, and NK cells) as well as nerve-associated corneal epithelial cells (Buela and Hendricks, 2015; Chucair-Elliott et al., 2017b; Gao et al., 2016a; Koyama and Hill, 2016; Liu et al., 2017; Royer et al., 2018; Seyed-Razavi et al., 2014; Stepp et al., 2017).

claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stepp et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Complement-mediated damage to corneal epithelial cells may have a direct impact on sensory nerves.

claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the evidence of membrane fusion between nerves and epithelial cells.

claims.claim: This is the first report documenting loss of corneal mechano-sensory function in ocular GVHD.
claims.source: Although corneal nerve damage is an established pathology in animal models of HSV-1 infection (Chucair-Elliott et al., 2015; He et al., 2017b; Yun et al., 2014), this is the first report documenting loss of corneal mechano-sensory function in ocular GVHD.
claims.evidence: This is a novel finding of the study.

claims.claim: Patients rarely exhibit neurological manifestations of GVHD affecting other tissues/organs.
claims.source: Notably, patients rarely exhibit neurological manifestations of GVHD affecting other tissues/organs (Grauer et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grauer et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Corneal sensation loss may provide a clinical benchmark for initiation of targeted therapies to curb progression of ocular GVHD in patients.
claims.source: Corneal sensation loss may provide a clinical benchmark for initiation of targeted therapies to curb progression of ocular GVHD in patients.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about potential clinical applications.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to He et al., 2017a and Tepelus et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Complement C3 is a known driver of systemic GVHD.
claims.source: Complement C3 is a known driver of systemic GVHD (Kwan et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2014; Seignez et al., 2017), and our data show that aberrant complement pathway activation also contributes to the pathogenesis of ocular GVHD including corneal sensation loss.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Aberrant complement pathway activation contributes to the pathogenesis of ocular GVHD including corneal sensation loss.
claims.source: Complement C3 is a known driver of systemic GVHD (Kwan et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2014; Seignez et al., 2017), and our data show that aberrant complement pathway activation also contributes to the pathogenesis of ocular GVHD including corneal sensation loss.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from the GVHD model.

claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kotimaa et al., 2016.

results.result: C3 deficiency preserves corneal sensation and innervation during HSV-1 infection despite similar or elevated viral loads. C3-/- mice maintained corneal sensation while WT mice lost sensation by days 5-8 post-infection. Viral titers were similar at day 3 but elevated in C3-/- mice by day 7, yet C3-/- corneas showed T cell infiltration without widespread denervation.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C32 provide converging evidence from sensation measurements (C25-C26), viral titer quantification (C27-C28), and microscopy/flow cytometry (C29-C31) demonstrating that C3 deficiency preserves corneal sensation independent of viral burden. The data are internally consistent and support the conclusion (C32) that sensation loss involves a C3-dependent inflammatory process.

results.result: C3 deficiency does not impair T cell priming, expansion, recruitment, or functional responses during HSV-1 infection. Chemokine expression, T cell expansion in draining lymph nodes, and IFNγ production upon restimulation were comparable between WT and C3-/- mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 demonstrate through multiple independent assays (chemokine measurement, flow cytometry, functional assays) that C3-/- T cells exhibit normal responses. This addresses a potential confounding explanation for the sensation phenotype and strengthens the conclusion that C3 acts independently of T cell function.

results.result: Both C3 and T cells are individually necessary and interdependent for corneal sensation loss during HSV-1 infection. TCRα-/- mice (lacking T cells) did not develop sensation loss despite having C3. Adoptive transfer of T cells from either WT or C3-/- donors into TCRα-/- recipients restored sensation loss, demonstrating that C3-/- T cells are functionally competent and that host C3 is required.
results.evaluation: The adoptive transfer experiments (C37-C38) provide strong evidence for interdependence by showing that neither C3 alone (in TCRα-/- mice) nor T cells alone (in C3-/- mice) are sufficient. The ability of C3-/- T cells to induce sensation loss in C3-sufficient recipients (C38-C39) demonstrates that T cell-intrinsic C3 is not required, supporting the conclusion of interdependence (C40-C41).

results.result: Antigen-specific CD4+ T cells, but not CD8+ T cells, are necessary to drive corneal sensation loss during HSV-1 infection. Only CD4+ T cell transfer restored sensation loss in TCRα-/- mice. OT-II mice with OVA-specific CD4+ T cells did not develop sensation loss despite T cell activation and corneal infiltration. Active HSV-1 infection was required, as mock infection did not induce sensation loss.
results.evaluation: The adoptive transfer experiments (C42) and OT-II experiments (C43) provide clear evidence for CD4+ T cell specificity. The mock infection control (C44) rules out non-specific inflammation from corneal injury. Together, these claims establish that antigen-specific CD4+ T cells are necessary (C45-C46), though the mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.

results.result: HSV-1 infection upregulates complement effectors (C3, C5, C3ar1, C5ar1) without proportional upregulation of regulatory components, creating an imbalance that favors local complement activation in the cornea.
results.evaluation: Gene expression data (C47-C48) demonstrate differential upregulation of effectors versus regulators. The inference that this favors complement activation (C49) is reasonable given established complement biology. However, protein-level confirmation and functional validation of pathway activation would strengthen this result.

results.result: Multiple cell types contribute to local C3 production during HSV-1 infection, including CSF1R+ leukocytes (the primary leukocyte source) and EpCAM+ corneal epithelial cells. Whole cornea preparations showed higher C3 expression than individual cell fractions, suggesting contributions from multiple cell types.
results.evaluation: The cell fractionation and expression analysis (C96-C99) provide direct evidence for multiple cellular sources of C3. The observation that whole cornea expression exceeds individual fractions (C99) supports the conclusion of multiple contributors (C100). However, quantitative assessment of relative contributions from each cell type would strengthen this result.

results.result: Pharmacologic C3 depletion with topical cobra venom factor (CVF) preserves corneal sensation during HSV-1 infection through localized complement inhibition. CVF treatment maintained baseline corneal C3 levels, reduced inflammation and leukocyte infiltration, and preserved sensation without affecting systemic C3 or T cell responses in lymphoid organs.
results.evaluation: The CVF experiments (C51-C56) provide proof-of-concept for therapeutic intervention. The localized effect (C53, C104) and lack of systemic T cell impact (C59) support specificity. The reduced viral titers in CVF-treated animals (C58) are unexpected and require further investigation. The therapeutic speculation (C60, C102) is reasonable but requires additional validation in established disease.

results.result: The allergic eye disease (AED) model shows CD4+ T cell infiltration without corneal sensation loss or frank nerve damage, demonstrating context-specificity of the C3/CD4+ T cell-mediated neuropathy. Despite clinical signs of allergy and T cell infiltration, corneal nerve density was preserved.
results.evaluation: The AED experiments (C61-C66) provide a critical negative control demonstrating that T cell infiltration alone is insufficient for sensation loss (C121). This supports the context-dependency of the pathology (C122). The differential T helper polarization (Th2/Th17 in AED vs Th1 in HSV-1/GVHD) may explain the difference, though this requires further investigation.

results.result: Corneal sensation loss occurs early in ocular GVHD and is instigated by allogeneic CD4+ T cells. Progressive sensation loss was observed following transfer of CD4+ T cells (with or without CD8+ T cells), accompanied by reduced corneal nerve density and external signs of ocular disease. This is the first report of corneal mechano-sensory dysfunction in ocular GVHD.
results.evaluation: The GVHD experiments (C67-C70) demonstrate CD4+ T cell-dependent sensation loss using adoptive transfer. The novelty claim (C71, C163) appears justified given the literature citations. This extends the C3/CD4+ T cell axis to a second disease model, strengthening the generalizability of the findings.

results.result: Local CVF treatment preserves corneal sensation and nerve integrity in ocular GVHD despite systemic disease progression. CVF preserved sensation in both sexes but only reduced other ocular surface manifestations in females. Systemic disease scores and inverted CD4:CD8 ratios confirmed GVHD development in all groups.
results.evaluation: The GVHD CVF experiments (C72-C77) demonstrate therapeutic efficacy in a second disease model, supporting the proof-of-concept (C79). The sex-specific effects on non-sensory outcomes (C77, C172) are intriguing but incompletely explained. The speculation about insufficient C3 depletion (C173) is reasonable but requires validation. The preservation of sensation despite systemic disease (C75) suggests a local mechanism.

results.result: The differential T helper polarization across disease models (Th2/Th17 in AED vs Th1 in HSV-1/GVHD) may explain the context-specificity of complement-mediated nerve damage. Th1 cytokines such as IFNγ, IL-2, and lymphotoxin-alpha may be important in coordinating sensation loss.
results.evaluation: While the differential polarization is documented by citations (C123-C124), the mechanistic link to sensation loss (C125) is speculative. The hypothesis is reasonable given the correlation between Th1 responses and sensation loss, but direct experimental evidence testing the role of specific cytokines is lacking. This represents an important future direction.

results.result: Complement has dual roles in HSV-1 infection: enhancing viral clearance while mediating maladaptive nerve damage. HSV-1 can evade C3 activation through glycoprotein C (gC), and neuronal cells are more resistant to complement-mediated damage than epithelial cells. C3 is involved in keratitis progression and nerve retraction but likely does not contribute to complete elimination of infected nerves.
results.evaluation: The discussion of complement's dual role is well-supported by citations (C127-C131) and consistent with the experimental data showing preserved sensation in C3-/- mice despite elevated viral loads. The inference about maladaptive host defense (C132) is reasonable. However, the conclusion about nerve elimination (C135) relies partly on cited data about viral latency (C134) rather than direct experimental evidence in the current study.

results.result: The role of preexisting immunity in complement-mediated nerve damage during recurrent HSV-1 infection remains incompletely understood. While vaccinated animals did not exhibit sensation loss, C3d deposition was present in the corneal epithelium, and C3 is essential for antibody-dependent viral clearance.
results.evaluation: This result identifies an important limitation (C136) and cites relevant prior work (C137-C139). However, the current study uses immunologically naive mice, so the claims about recurrent infection are based on citations rather than new experimental data. The speculation about complement proteostasis imbalance (C141) is reasonable but requires experimental validation in the context of recurrent infection.

results.result: The precise cellular and molecular mechanisms of complement-mediated nerve damage remain to be identified. The working hypothesis involves sublytic MAC deposition damaging nerves, which are then cleared by T cell-activated phagocytes or epithelial cells. Membrane fusion between nerves and epithelial cells may enable direct complement-mediated damage.
results.evaluation: The mechanistic hypotheses (C159, C162) are reasonable given the data, but remain speculative. The identification of knowledge gaps (C142, C158) is appropriate. The proposed mechanisms involving MAC deposition and phagocytic clearance are plausible but lack direct experimental evidence in the current study. Future work with more specific mechanistic tools (e.g., MAC-deficient mice, phagocyte depletion) is needed.

results.result: CSF1R+ macrophages/monocytes are recruited early during HSV-1 infection and are associated with nerve damage. CD4+ T cells coordinate sensation loss, but this is not dependent on T cell-intrinsic C3 production. The tempo of sensation loss is consistent across models once initiated, with slight delays in adoptive transfer models reflecting lymphopenic status.
results.evaluation: The identification of CSF1R+ cells as C3 sources (C145) connects to prior work on their role in nerve damage. The adoptive transfer data (C147) clearly demonstrate that T cell-intrinsic C3 is not required. The kinetic analysis (C148-C149) provides insight into the temporal dynamics and the role of T cell numbers. These observations support the overall model of C3/CD4+ T cell interdependence (C150).

results.result: The role of intracellular C3 and anaphylatoxin receptor signaling in murine T cell responses during HSV-1 infection is unclear. Mice lack CD46, and ex vivo data show no defect in IFNγ production by C3-/- T cells, though in vitro polarization studies have shown reduced IFNγ. Local anaphylatoxin signaling may modulate T cell function in the inflamed cornea.
results.evaluation: The discussion appropriately addresses species differences (C152) and conflicting literature (C154-C156). The ex vivo data (C154) support normal T cell function in C3-/- mice, but the speculation about local anaphylatoxin signaling (C157) lacks direct experimental evidence. Experiments with anaphylatoxin receptor-deficient mice would be needed to test this hypothesis.

results.result: Corneal sensation loss may serve as an early clinical biomarker for ocular GVHD progression. Patients rarely exhibit neurological GVHD in other tissues, and corneal nerve remodeling has been documented in ocular GVHD patients. Clinical studies measuring corneal sensation in HSCT patients are warranted.
results.evaluation: The translational speculation (C165-C167) is reasonable given the animal data showing early sensation loss (C166) and clinical evidence of nerve remodeling (C168). However, these remain hypotheses requiring clinical validation. The rarity of neurological GVHD in other tissues (C164) suggests the cornea may be uniquely susceptible, but the mechanism is unclear.

results.result: Complement C3 contributes to both systemic and ocular GVHD pathogenesis. Sex differences in complement activity may explain differential therapeutic responses to CVF treatment. Sensory nerve involvement may represent a unique therapeutic target in ocular GVHD.
results.evaluation: The role of C3 in systemic GVHD is well-established by citations (C169), and the current data extend this to ocular manifestations (C170). The sex difference observation (C174) is supported by citation and may explain the dimorphic CVF response. The therapeutic speculation (C175) is reasonable given the data showing sensation preservation with CVF treatment.

results.result: CVF is an appropriate tool for proof-of-concept complement inhibition studies. Purified CVF depletes C3 through stable convertase formation and effector consumption. Topical administration is safe and does not affect T cell responses systemically. CVF preserved sensation in both HSV-1 and GVHD models.
results.evaluation: The methodological justification for CVF use is well-supported by citations (C178-C180, C183-C184) and experimental observations (C181-C182, C186). The lack of systemic T cell effects (C186) and localized action support the validity of the approach. The consistent efficacy across models (C190) strengthens the proof-of-concept. However, CVF is not clinically applicable, so translation requires development of alternative complement inhibitors.

results.result: Complement activation in the cornea is a double-edged sword with both protective (antimicrobial) and pathological (nerve damage) effects. Low-level complement turnover occurs in healthy corneas and may contribute to the paucibacterial ocular surface. Elucidating the mechanisms regulating these effects will advance drug development.
results.evaluation: The dual role concept (C193) is well-supported by the experimental data and citations. The discussion of baseline complement activity (C194-C195) provides important context. The identification of knowledge gaps (C196) and future directions (C197) is appropriate. However, the specific mechanisms distinguishing protective from pathological complement activation remain to be elucidated.

results.result: Species differences in complement regulation between mice and humans must be considered for translational potential. Genetic polymorphisms in complement genes (complotype) influence disease susceptibility in AMD and may similarly affect ocular surface disease susceptibility.
results.evaluation: The discussion of species differences (C198) and genetic variation (C199-C200) is well-supported by citations and represents important considerations for translation. The speculation about complotype in ocular surface diseases (C201) is reasonable by analogy to AMD but requires experimental validation. These represent important caveats for interpreting the translational potential of the findings.

results.result: The study demonstrates successful prophylactic complement inhibition in two T cell-dependent corneal disease models. Future work is needed to determine therapeutic efficacy in established disease. Topical complement-targeted therapeutics may control ocular surface diseases without systemic risks.
results.evaluation: The summary of achievements (C202) accurately reflects the experimental data. The identification of the prophylactic limitation (C203) is an important caveat, as clinical application would likely require treatment of established disease. The therapeutic speculation (C204) is reasonable given the proof-of-concept data, but requires development of clinically applicable complement inhibitors and validation in therapeutic (not just prophylactic) settings.
